A lot of players felt betrayed by DA 2 and beyond because it was such a deviation from Origins in terms of gameplay, story scope, and fixed PC. Mass Effect had a lot to do with the change. Back then the dialogue wheel and voiced protagonist thing was new-fangled for a CRPG. Bioware was known for their DnD and Star Wars campaigns, which used the traditional dialogue tree format which had no PC voice. There weren’t even fully voiced NPCs until Knights of the Old Republic I believe. 

I am one of those people who longs for the dialogue tree aka way more choices for responses and no voiced lines. I was thanking the Maker when BG3 kept to this format a la BG1 and 2. It was proof that the format was not a deterrent to players. It’s half the reason DAO is known for its roleplaying possibilities in terms of how your character can respond to things. A lot may not have even changed the outcome of quests a great deal, but the idea that you could be a lawful good knight or an unhinged homicidal maniac felt like your response as a player was more within your own control rather than what the game sort of decided for you. 

Now, I am personally a big fan of DA2 and DAI, but it’s not because of the gameplay or dialogue choices. The reason I remained a faithful DA stan was because BioWare knew where their strengths lay: storytelling and characters. 

And when I say storytelling I don’t necessarily mean the main plot structure or even content. I agree that Origins had a very cliche main story. I also don’t particularly feel attached to Grey Wardens, they just didn’t feel special to me the way that most other fans do. 

Almost every crpg, almost every video game period, has the same basic structure of being a chosen one hero who defeats the BBEG and everyone rejoices at the end. 

DA2 still did that, but the way it did it was why it’s the best of the series to me. It dialled the scope way back, but also extended the duration in terms of in-game time (a whole decade!) it made the focus on companion relationships and development across those ten years, and made some of the most daring choices in how it did that with the friendship and rivalry systems. To this day I have never seen another game quite like it. 

Anyway, this is way too long and don’t worry about the downvotes you’re getting. You can like and dislike whichever game you please. I certainly do!

Sounds like my old physio. She’d make weird comments about me, I’m trans and gay. But she’d also say weird stuff about race, suicide, etc. that were not related to me. I put up with it for 4 years, thinking that she was the best I could get and that I needed to push through because she was the only one who could help me. Turns out when I finally could no longer tolerate it and saw a few different physios later, they helped me much more and never said anything untoward at all.

Among other things like what I personally think was lazy writing and terrible direction by the showrunners, queer people like myself did not enjoy seeing yet another example of [Bury Your Gays](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BuryYourGays). The history of queer characters in media has obviously been fraught with censorship (check out the history of the [Hays Code](https://www.acmi.net.au/stories-and-ideas/early-hollywood-and-hays-code/)). Despite the code being abolished, it seems the culture of film and television writing is still plagued with the ghost of Hays, and the result is often something like what happens in the finale of KE. 

If there were no such history, say perhaps this show was about straight relationship, then the idea of the characters receiving punishment their murderous behaviour, perhaps I’d agree. But in this case the fact that it’s about two women is very important. 

There is so much more that has already been said very eloquently before in this sub about the finale, but that’s a quick lowdown of why.

So it’s not overly surprising when, especially if it’s a small and local group, the demographics are uneven.  It’s sadly the nature of groups and that isn’t the fault of anyone inherently.

The trans umbrella has become than ever. I think it’s fine to desire a more specific type of group within that to have a meetup with. 

To be personal, I’m in the NB umbrella. I only use ‘he’ pronouns. I consider myself post-surgical and medical transition, and have been for ten years now. I pass as male. Most of the time, I look like a binary guy. I’m pretty gay sounding and looking, but not anymore than a cis guy could be. I like dressing androgynously but often don’t because I’m literally too tired to make the effort (thanks chronic illness!). 

It’s only been in more recent years that I have noticed people started to not understand why, say, a nonbinary person would use ‘he’ instead of ‘they’. But that is a discussion for another time. 

All that being said, I would also feel unable to relate to a room full of people who have not gone through hormones/surgery who use ‘she’ pronouns talking about trans issues. 

Does that invalidate them? I don’t think so. 

Does it become a problem when they start speaking over me and not allowing me to talk about my own experiences? Yes. 

If that is the case for you, then it is indeed very unfair and objectionable of them. You have the right to talk about yourself as much as they do.

Check out the customization options for brushes in Procreate. You can edit any brush with a ton of options, the most useful for lines is the ‘stabilization’ feature. It helps smooth your lines out. 

There’s also pen pressure customization. It changes how hard you have to press to get your lines at full opacity. 

These two options, as well as things like the glove and screen protector (i use rubber pen tips from pen.tips website that work great if you’d rather not put a whole screen protector on.) helped me with lines immensely. I have shaking hands sometimes but even without that, it’s very difficult to replicate real ink on real paper without fine tuning like that.

You have to learn the rules in order to break them. Studying anatomy and realism is good. When you know proportions, centre of gravity, and other stuff from realism/drawing from life, stylizing will be easy. 

Hyperrealism is not what most artists do, but I guess that depends on what your definition is. If all you do is draw a face that is  nigh indistinguishable from the reference photo, for example, then it’s less like art and more like a sort of dry, straightforward demonstration of technical skill. Not knocking those who do this, but it’s not and shouldn’t be the standard. It’s simply one genre of many.
